hook: He started *washing dishes* at 17. Now he owns the *steakhouse on 125th*.
dek: PB Brasserie Steak House, Harlem. Chef Cisse's French and African steakhouse: dry-aged steaks, three tiled arches and jazz on Wednesdays.

slides.label: The chef
slides.text: Chef *Elhadji Cisse* came to New York from Senegal at 17. His first job: *washing dishes*. He never went to culinary school. "I learned from dishwasher to all the way up."

slides.label: The rise
slides.text: He worked downtown "with all these great chefs, from *Jean-Georges to Daniel*." Now culinary school grads come to him. "I teach them how to cook. *I'm serious.*"

slides.label: The empire
slides.text: Today he runs *four Harlem restaurants*: Ponty Bistro, Renaissance Harlem, Harlem Cafe and his biggest yet, *PB Brasserie* at 60 W 125th St.

slides.label: The concept
slides.text: A *brasserie steakhouse*: French and African cooking, steaks that are mostly *dry-aged*. "I always wanted to have a fine dining in Harlem."

slides.label: The room
slides.text: Three *blue-tiled arches* over a marble bar, a velvet lounge, a private room for 25 to 30 and *jazz every Wednesday*.

slides.label: The order
slides.text: His favorite cut: *the ribeye*. "I'm a ribeye guy." The best seller: *lobster spaghetti*. We added escargot, calamari and mac and cheese.

slides.label: Harlem is home
slides.text: Almost 30 years in Harlem. "My kids were born in *Harlem Hospital*. Harlem is *everything* for us."

slides.label: The Den's take
slides.text: "*Very upscale*, but you can still feel like it's *Harlem*." The steak is worth the trip. The room, the music and the service are why you come back.

cta_line: Before you go downtown for a steak, *come to 125th*.

caption_linkedin:
He started as a dishwasher at 17. Today he runs four restaurants in Harlem.

Chef Elhadji Cisse came to New York from Senegal and never went to culinary school. He learned every station instead: dish pit, line, the floor, downtown kitchens with chefs from Jean-Georges to Daniel. "Every place I run, I was the main guy," he told us. So when he opened his own: "When I come to the business, I know what to do."

Now culinary school graduates come to him to learn. And his newest, PB Brasserie Steak House on 125th Street, puts fine dining where he says Harlem has too little of it.

The lesson for any founder: learn the work before you run the business.

Did you learn your industry from the ground up, or from the top down?
